newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-rightist sees boom if suburbs "explode".
newsitem.headline: French far-rightist sees boom if suburbs "explode".

text.p: Far right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, riding a wave of publicity ahead of his National Front's congress this weekend, said on Thursday his party could boom if poor city suburbs "exploded" or Algerian refugees flocked to France.

The mayor of Strasbourg, which is reluctantly hosting the conference, said Le Pen's presence could prompt clashes with leftists planning to draw at least 20,000 people from across France for an anti-fascist demonstration. She appealed for calm.

Some 2,200 delegates will attend the three-day congress, due to reelect Le Pen, adopt a manifesto for next year's general election and propose bills to restore the death penalty and send immigrants back to their country of origin, which National Front parliamentarians would propose if they won seats.
Although Le Pen won 15 percent of votes in the 1995 presidential election, his movement has no seats in parliament because of the twin-ballot constituency voting system.

Ruling centre-right parties and opposition Socialists are at loggerheads on how to counter the anti-immigrant party's rise, highlighted by its capture of a fourth southern city in local elections in February and controversy over a new law against illegal immigration.

"The Vitrolles victory means that in any constituency where the Front has more than 25 or 30 percent today it could, if an exceptional event occurred -- and it will -- enjoy a popular groundswell in its favour," Le Pen told the newspaper Le Figaro.
"Just imagine a victory of the Islamic Salvation Front in Algeria, and the flight towards France of hundreds of thousands of Algerians...or an explosion in the suburbs," he said.
The party is strongest in southern France, in Paris' poor suburbs and in Alsace in the northeast, where the congress will be held.
Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann, a Socialist, has called in national police reinforcements to avert feared clashes between demonstrators and far-right militants.
"I have repeatedly appealed for calm...I have written to the Interior Ministry to request sufficent police forces to ensure people's security," Trautmann told Europe-1 radio.

"Le Pen has decided not to go the cathedral because he said that his presence might cause clashes. That is the first time that Mr Le Pen has publicly recognised that he is himself a cause of clashes and that choosing to come to Strasbourg creates problems," she said.
Front number two Bruno Megret said violence was very likely because "establishment thugs" were bent on causing trouble. Delegates will be asked to remain in the congress centre.
Trautmann will lead a Saturday march against Le Pen, who has filed a lawsuit against persons unknown for allegedly conspiring to disrupt the congress.

British writer Salman Rushdie, who is under an Iranian death threat, told a meeting of the Writers' Parliament in Strasbourg that Le Pen should be allowed "to express his opinions and demonstrate they are harmful".
"Freedom of expression starts in debate with people with whom you don't agree. That doesn't mean one mustn't react. But citizens have to be trusted," Rushdie said.

Leaders of the ruling centre-right coalition denounced the Front's policies at a public rally in Strasbourg on Wednesday night but also criticised the Left's response, saying they would not join Saturday's demonstration.
Le Pen has chosen to hold the congress in the region where he won his biggest score in the 1995 presidential election. He polled 25 percent in Alsace compared to 15 percent nationwide.
